opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, at the time I took it pretty hard. I was a kid, and the school sorted everyone by their entrance results, so Class 1 was the top class and Class 4 was... well, not the top. Everyone knew what the numbers meant. Nobody had to say it out loud.

My first reaction was something like embarrassment, and a bit of confusion too, because up to that point I'd always been the kid who was "good at math." Suddenly there was this very clear external signal saying: actually, relative to these people, you're not that special. That was a strange feeling to have so young.

But looking back, I think I interpreted it in a way that ended up being useful. I didn't read it as "I'm not a math person." I read it more as "this is a snapshot of where I am right now, on this particular kind of test." Olympiad problems reward a certain kind of training, and a lot of the kids in the top classes had simply started earlier or had more exposure to those problem types. So part of me thought, okay, this is information, not a verdict.

And there was also something kind of freeing about it. When you're in Class 4, nobody expects much from you. You don't have the pressure of defending a position. You can just be curious, try weird approaches, get things wrong. I spent a lot of time just playing with problems I found interesting, rather than drilling to stay on top.

I think that experience shaped how I see rankings in general, even later on. Placements, test scores, those things measure something real, but they're very narrow and very time-bound. What matters more is whether you keep showing up to the problems. So, at the time it stung, but now I'm actually kind of grateful I started there.

r001.rationale: The response says she felt less special relative to the other students, but explicitly says she did not interpret the placement as meaning she was not a math person. It does not communicate the criterion’s core interpretation.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, at the time I just took it as a fact about where I was, not a verdict on where I'd end up. The school sorted kids into classes by level, and Class 4 was pretty far from the top. I remember looking at the kids in Class 1 and thinking they were a different species, like they'd been born knowing things I had to fight for.

But I think the placement actually helped me, because it meant nobody expected much. There was no pressure to perform, so I could just be curious. I'd go home and redo the problems I'd gotten wrong, and over time I started noticing that the gap between me and the kids above wasn't really talent, it was hours. They had simply seen more problems. That was a very freeing realization for a kid, because hours are something you can control.

So I interpreted it as a starting line rather than a label. And looking back, I'm a little grateful for it. If I'd started at the top, I might never have learned that the climb itself was the part I enjoyed.

r001.rationale: She describes Class 4 as far from the top and initially sees top students as unusually gifted, but says she took her own placement as a starting line, not a verdict. She does not clearly say it showed she was not naturally gifted at math.
